imo-isl-2021-a1.title: Contradiction with a geometric growth
imo-isl-2021-a1.body:
The statement is meant for $n\ge1$ (for $n=0$ the set $A=\{0,1\}$ has only two elements), so assume $n\ge1$.

List the elements of $A$ in increasing order: $x_0<x_1<\dots<x_{4n+1}$, and put $c=x_{4n+1}$. Suppose, for contradiction, that no triple works. For every $i=0,1,\dots,4n-1$ the triple $a=x_i<b=x_{i+1}<c$ then satisfies $c+2a\le3b$, which can be rewritten as
$$3(c-x_{i+1})\le 2(c-x_i),\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad c-x_i\ge\tfrac32\,(c-x_{i+1}).$$
Applying this for $i=4n-1,4n-2,\dots,0$ gives by induction
$$c-x_i\ge\left(\tfrac32\right)^{4n-i}(c-x_{4n})\quad(0\le i\le 4n).$$
For $i=0$, using $c-x_{4n}\ge1$ (distinct integers):
$$c-x_0\ge\left(\tfrac32\right)^{4n}=\left(\tfrac{81}{16}\right)^n>5^n,$$
because $\frac{81}{16}=5.0625>5$. But $0\le x_0<c\le5^n$ gives $c-x_0\le5^n$, a contradiction.

Hence there exist $a<b<c$ in $A$ with $c+2a>3b$. ∎

imo-isl-2021-a1.title: Pigeonhole on geometric intervals
imo-isl-2021-a1.body:
Let $c=\max A$ (assume $n\ge1$; then $c\ge 4n+1\ge1$). For $k=0,1,\dots,4n-1$ define the intervals
$$I_k=\Big[\big(1-(2/3)^k\big)c,\ \big(1-(2/3)^{k+1}\big)c\Big).$$
They are disjoint, consecutive, start at $0$ and end at $\big(1-(16/81)^n\big)c>c-(1/5)^nc\ge c-1$. Every element of $A\setminus\{c\}$ is an integer in $[0,c-1]$, so it lies in some $I_k$. There are $4n+1$ such elements and $4n$ intervals, so two of them, $a<b$, lie in the same $I_k$. Then
$$c+2a\ge c+2\big(1-(2/3)^k\big)c=3\big(1-(2/3)^{k+1}\big)c>3b,$$
as required. ∎

imo-isl-2021-a2.title: Pair row $i$ with row $n+1-i$
imo-isl-2021-a2.body:
**A floor inequality.** If $x+y$ is an integer, then
$$\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor\ge x+y-1,$$
with equality when $x\notin\mathbb Z$ and with $\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor=x+y$ when $x\in\mathbb Z$. Indeed, if $x\in\mathbb Z$ then $y\in\mathbb Z$ too and the floors change nothing; otherwise $\{x\}+\{y\}$ is a positive integer less than $2$, so it equals $1$.

**Estimate.** Let $S$ be the sum of the table. For fixed $j$, the map $i\mapsto n+1-i$ permutes the rows, so
$$2S=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{(n+1-i)j}{n+1}\right\rfloor\right).$$
The two numbers inside add up to $j$, an integer, so each bracket is at least $j-1$:
$$2S\ge\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n(j-1)=n\cdot\frac{n(n-1)}2,\qquad S\ge\frac14n^2(n-1).$$
Equality holds if and only if every bracket equals $j-1$, i.e. no number $\frac{ij}{n+1}$ with $1\le i,j\le n$ is an integer.

**When does equality hold?**
- If $n+1$ is prime, then $n+1\nmid ij$ for $1\le i,j\le n$, so $S=\frac14n^2(n-1)$.
- If $n+1$ is composite, write $n+1=ab$ with $2\le a,b\le n$. Then for $i=a,\ j=b$ the number $\frac{ij}{n+1}=1$ is an integer, the inequality is strict and $S>\frac14n^2(n-1)$.

**Answer: all $n$ such that $n+1$ is a prime.** ∎

imo-isl-2021-a3.title: Cyclic blocks and a logarithmic lower bound
imo-isl-2021-a3.body:
Let $k$ be the integer with $2^k\le n<2^{k+1}$.

**A permutation achieving $k+1$.** Split $\{1,\dots,n\}$ into the $k+1$ blocks $[1,1],[2,3],[4,7],\dots,[2^{k-1},2^k-1],[2^k,n]$. On a block $[p,q]$ (where always $q<2p$) define
$$a_p=q,\qquad a_i=i-1\ \ (p<i\le q),$$
i.e. $(a_p,a_{p+1},\dots,a_q)=(q,p,p+1,\dots,q-1)$. This is a permutation of each block, hence of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. On the block the contribution is
$$\left\lfloor\frac qp\right\rfloor+\sum_{i=p+1}^{q}\left\lfloor\frac{i-1}{i}\right\rfloor=1+0=1,$$
since $p\le q<2p$. So the total is $k+1$.

**Lower bound.** *Lemma.* For positive integers $a,b$: $\left\lfloor\frac ab\right\rfloor\ge\log_2\frac{a+1}b$.
*Proof.* Let $t=\lfloor a/b\rfloor\ge0$. Then $a<b(t+1)$, so $a+1\le b(t+1)$ and $\frac{a+1}b\le t+1\le2^t$ (as $2^t\ge t+1$ for integers $t\ge0$). Take $\log_2$. $\square$

Summing the lemma over $i$:
$$\sum_{i=1}^n\left\lfloor\frac{a_i}i\right\rfloor\ge\sum_{i=1}^n\log_2(a_i+1)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log_2 i=\log_2\frac{2\cdot3\cdots(n+1)}{1\cdot2\cdots n}=\log_2(n+1),$$
because $a_1+1,\dots,a_n+1$ is a permutation of $2,\dots,n+1$. Since $n+1>2^k$, the sum is $>k$, and being an integer it is at least $k+1$.

**Answer: the minimum is $\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor+1$.** ∎

imo-isl-2021-a3.title: Lower bound by covering the powers of $2$
imo-isl-2021-a3.body:
Here is another proof of the lower bound; the construction is as in the first solution. Let $P=\{1,2,4,\dots,2^k\}$, the powers of $2$ in $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Call an index $i$ *good* if $a_i\ge i$, and then call $[i,a_i]$ a good interval.

*The good intervals cover $\{1,\dots,n\}$.* Take $x$ and follow its cycle $c_0=x,\ c_1=a_{c_0},\ c_2=a_{c_1},\dots$ in the permutation. The walk eventually returns to $x$, so there is a first index $j\ge0$ with $c_{j+1}=a_{c_j}\ge x$. Put $i=c_j$. If $j=0$ then $i=x$; if $j>0$ then $i=c_j=a_{c_{j-1}}<x$ by the choice of $j$. In both cases $i\le x\le a_i$, so $i$ is good and $x$ is covered by $[i,a_i]$.

*A good interval containing $p$ powers of $2$ contributes at least $p$.* If $[i,a_i]$ contains $p\ge1$ powers of two, the largest is at least $2^{p-1}$ times the smallest, so $\frac{a_i}i\ge2^{p-1}\ge p$ and $\lfloor a_i/i\rfloor\ge p$.

Since the good intervals cover the $k+1$ elements of $P$,
$$\sum_i\left\lfloor\frac{a_i}i\right\rfloor\ge\sum_{i\text{ good}}\big|[i,a_i]\cap P\big|\ge|P|=k+1.$$
∎

imo-isl-2021-a5.title: Compare each term with a telescoping difference
imo-isl-2021-a5.body:
Let $s_k=a_1+\dots+a_k$ ($s_0=0$, $s_n=1$). Since $n\ge2$ and all $a_i>0$, we have $0<a_k<1$. We claim that for every $k$
$$\frac{a_k}{1-a_k}\,s_{k-1}^2<\frac{s_k^3-s_{k-1}^3}{3}.\tag{1}$$
Write $a=a_k$, $s=s_{k-1}$, so $s_k=s+a\le1$. Then $\frac{(s+a)^3-s^3}{3}=s^2a+sa^2+\frac{a^3}3$, and multiplying (1) by $1-a>0$ it becomes
$$as^2<(1-a)\Big(s^2a+sa^2+\frac{a^3}3\Big).$$
The difference of the two sides is
$$(1-a)\Big(s^2a+sa^2+\frac{a^3}3\Big)-as^2=sa^2(1-s-a)+\frac{a^3}{3}(1-a),$$
where $sa^2(1-s-a)\ge0$ because $s+a=s_k\le1$, and $\frac{a^3}3(1-a)>0$. This proves (1).

Adding (1) for $k=1,\dots,n$, the right-hand sides telescope:
$$\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{a_k}{1-a_k}s_{k-1}^2<\frac{s_n^3-s_0^3}{3}=\frac13.$$
∎

imo-isl-2021-a5.title: Splitting a term increases the sum
imo-isl-2021-a5.body:
Let $S(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ denote the left-hand side and $s=a_1+\dots+a_{i-1}$. Replacing $a_i$ by two numbers $a_i/2,a_i/2$ (keeping the order) changes $S$ by
$$\frac{a_i/2}{1-a_i/2}\Big(s^2+\big(s+\tfrac{a_i}2\big)^2\Big)-\frac{a_i}{1-a_i}s^2
=a_i\,\frac{(1-a_i-s)\,s\,a_i+(1-a_i)\,a_i^2/4}{(2-a_i)(1-a_i)}>0$$
(direct computation; the terms after position $i$ are unchanged since their prefix sums are unchanged). So halving terms strictly increases $S$. Repeating this, all terms become arbitrarily small while $S$ increases; for a subdivision $0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_N=1$ with mesh $\to0$, $S=\sum\frac{\Delta t}{1-\Delta t}t_{j-1}^2\to\int_0^1x^2\,dx=\frac13$. Since the starting value is strictly smaller than every later value, it is $<\frac13$. ∎

imo-isl-2021-a7.title: A quadratic identity and a square-root sum
imo-isl-2021-a7.body:
**Lemma 1.** If $a,b,c\ge0$ and $ab-c^2\ge1$, then $(a+2b)^2\ge(b+2c)^2+6$.

*Proof.* Expanding, $(a+2b)^2-(b+2c)^2=a^2+4ab+3b^2-4bc-4c^2=(a-b)^2+2(b-c)^2+6(ab-c^2)\ge6$. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** $\sqrt1+\sqrt2+\dots+\sqrt n>\frac23n^{3/2}$.

*Proof.* The function $u\mapsto(1+u)^{3/2}$ is strictly convex on $[-1,\infty)$, so it lies above its tangent at $0$: $(1+u)^{3/2}>1+\frac32u$ for $u\ne0$, $u\ge-1$. With $u=-\frac1k$ ($k\ge1$) and multiplying by $k^{3/2}$:
$$(k-1)^{3/2}>k^{3/2}-\tfrac32\sqrt k.$$
Summing over $k=1,\dots,n$ and telescoping: $0>n^{3/2}-\frac32\left(\sqrt1+\dots+\sqrt n\right)$. $\square$

**Main proof.** Put $y_i=2x_i+x_{i+1}\ge0$ for $i=0,1,\dots,n$. For $1\le i\le n$, apply Lemma 1 with $a=x_{i+1}$, $b=x_i$, $c=x_{i-1}$ (here $ab-c^2=x_ix_{i+1}-x_{i-1}^2\ge1$):
$$y_i^2=(x_{i+1}+2x_i)^2\ge(x_i+2x_{i-1})^2+6=y_{i-1}^2+6.$$
Since $y_0^2\ge0$, induction gives $y_i^2\ge6i$, i.e. $y_i\ge\sqrt{6i}$.

All $x_j$ are non-negative, and each $x_j$ appears in $y_1+\dots+y_n$ with total coefficient at most $3$, so
$$3(x_0+x_1+\dots+x_{n+1})\ge y_1+\dots+y_n\ge\sqrt6\left(\sqrt1+\dots+\sqrt n\right)>\sqrt6\cdot\frac23n^{3/2}.$$
Dividing by $3$ and using $\frac{\sqrt6}{3}\cdot\frac23=\frac{2\sqrt6}{9}=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3\sqrt3}$ and $\left(\frac{2n}3\right)^{3/2}=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3\sqrt3}\,n^{3/2}$, we get
$$x_0+\dots+x_{n+1}>\left(\frac{2n}3\right)^{3/2}.$$
∎

*Remark.* The constant is sharp: $x_i=\sqrt{2/3}\,(\sqrt i+1)$ satisfies the conditions, and its sum is $\left(\frac{2n}3\right)^{3/2}+O(n)$.

imo-isl-2021-a8.title: Constant or injective, then multiplicative, then $x^\tau$
imo-isl-2021-a8.body:
Write $E(a,b,c)$ for the equation, $P=ab^2+bc^2+ca^2$, $Q=a^2b+b^2c+c^2a$, and note the identity $P-Q=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$.

**These functions work.** Constants $\beta$ cancel on both sides. For $f(x)=x$ the equation is exactly the identity $P-Q=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$. For $f(x)=x^3$ we need $(a^3-b^3)(b^3-c^3)(c^3-a^3)=P^3-Q^3$. Let $\omega$ be a primitive cube root of unity. Expanding, $(a-\omega b)(b-\omega c)(c-\omega a)=\omega^2P-\omega Q=\omega^2(P-\omega^2Q)$, and similarly $(a-\omega^2b)(b-\omega^2c)(c-\omega^2a)=\omega(P-\omega Q)$. Since $x^3-y^3=(x-y)(x-\omega y)(x-\omega^2y)$, multiplying these with $(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)=P-Q$ gives $(a^3-b^3)(b^3-c^3)(c^3-a^3)=(P-Q)(P-\omega Q)(P-\omega^2Q)=P^3-Q^3$. Replacing $f$ by $-f$ changes the sign of both sides, so $\alpha=-1$ also works.

From now on let $f$ be a solution. Since $f+C$ is also a solution, assume $f(0)=0$.

**Step 1: $f\equiv0$ or $f$ is injective.** Let $\Theta=\{(a,b):f(a)=f(b)\}$. If $(a,b)\in\Theta$, then the left side of $E(a,b,x)$ vanishes, so
$$H_{a,b}(x):=\big(ab^2+bx^2+xa^2,\ a^2b+b^2x+x^2a\big)\in\Theta\quad\text{for all }x.$$
Suppose $(a,b)\in\Theta$ with $a\ne b$. The difference of the coordinates of $H_{a,b}(x)$ is $(a-b)(b-x)(x-a)$ and their sum is $(x^2+ab)(a+b)+x(a^2+b^2)$; both are non-zero polynomials in $x$ (the second has leading coefficient $a+b$, or equals $2a^2x\ne0$ if $a+b=0$). Choosing $x$ outside their finitely many roots gives $(\alpha,\beta)\in\Theta$ with $\alpha\ne\pm\beta$.

Now $E(t,1,0)$ reads $\big(f(t)-f(1)\big)f(1)\big(-f(t)\big)=f(t)-f(t^2)$. Its left side depends only on $f(t)$, so $f(\alpha)=f(\beta)$ gives $f(\alpha^2)=f(\beta^2)$, and $\alpha^2\ne\beta^2$. Since $\Theta$ is symmetric, we may assume $\alpha^2<\beta^2$. Repeating the squaring, $\big(\alpha^{2^j},\beta^{2^j}\big)\in\Theta$ for all $j\ge1$; if $\alpha=0$ these are $(0,\beta^{2^j})$, otherwise the ratio $(\beta^2/\alpha^2)^{2^{j-1}}$ tends to infinity. So we obtain $(\gamma,\delta)\in\Theta$ with $\delta>5\gamma\ge0$.

If $\gamma=0$ put $r=\delta$. If $\gamma>0$, the quadratic $\gamma x^2+\delta^2x+\delta\gamma^2=0$ has discriminant $\delta(\delta^3-4\gamma^3)>0$, and its root $x$ is negative (all coefficients are positive). Then $H_{\delta,\gamma}(x)=(0,r)$ for some $r$, and $0-r=(\delta-\gamma)(\gamma-x)(x-\delta)<0$, so $r\ne0$. Either way $(0,r)\in\Theta$ with $r\ne0$.

Next $H_{0,r}(x)=(rx^2,r^2x)\in\Theta$, so $f(rx^2)=f(r^2x)$ for all $x$; replacing $x$ by $-x$, $f(r^2x)=f(-r^2x)$, so $f$ is even: $(a,-a)\in\Theta$ for all $a$. Then
$$H_{a,-a}(x)=\big(a^3-ax^2+a^2x,\ -a^3+a^2x+ax^2\big)\in\Theta.$$
For $x=\varphi a$ with $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$ (so $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$) this is $\big(0,(1+\sqrt5)a^3\big)$. As $a$ ranges over $\mathbb R$, $(1+\sqrt5)a^3$ takes every real value, so $f\equiv f(0)=0$.

**Step 2: if $f$ is injective, then $f$ is odd and (after a sign change) $f(1)=1$.** $E(a,b,0)$ gives
$$f(a)f(b)\big(f(a)-f(b)\big)=f(a^2b)-f(ab^2).\tag{$\heartsuit$}$$
Let $\kappa=f(1)\ne0$. With $b=1$: $\kappa f(a)\big(f(a)-\kappa\big)=f(a^2)-f(a)$. Subtracting the same relation for $-a$:
$$\kappa\big(f(a)-f(-a)\big)\big(f(a)+f(-a)-\kappa\big)=f(-a)-f(a).$$
For $a\ne0$ injectivity allows division: $f(a)+f(-a)=\kappa-\kappa^{-1}=:\lambda$. Hence for $a,b\ne0$: $f(a)-f(b)=f(-b)-f(-a)$. Write ($\heartsuit$) for $(-a,-b)$ with $a,b\ne0$; its right side is $f(-a^2b)-f(-ab^2)=f(ab^2)-f(a^2b)$. Adding to ($\heartsuit$):
$$\big(f(a)-f(b)\big)\big(f(a)f(b)-f(-a)f(-b)\big)=0.$$
So for distinct non-zero $a,b$: $f(a)f(b)=(\lambda-f(a))(\lambda-f(b))$, i.e. $\lambda\big(\lambda-f(a)-f(b)\big)=0$. If $\lambda\ne0$, then $f(b)=\lambda-f(a)$ for all $b\ne0,a$, contradicting injectivity. So $\lambda=0$, $\kappa=\pm1$, and $f$ is odd. Replacing $f$ by $-f$ if necessary, $f(1)=1$.

**Step 3: $f$ is multiplicative and positive on $(0,\infty)$.** With $\kappa=1$ the relation for $b=1$ becomes $f(a^2)=f(a)^2$. Adding ($\heartsuit$) for $(a,b)$ and $(a,-b)$ (using oddness) gives $-2f(a)f(b)^2=-2f(ab^2)$, i.e. $f(ab^2)=f(a)f(b^2)$. Hence $f(ax)=f(a)f(x)$ for all $a$ and all $x\ge0$, and by oddness for all real $a,x$. Also $f(x)=f(\sqrt x)^2\ge0$ for $x\ge0$, and $f(x)>0$ for $x>0$ by injectivity.

**Step 4: $f(x)=x^\tau$ on $(0,\infty)$ with $\tau>0$.** Let $g(t)=\ln f(e^t)$; then $g$ is additive. *Fact:* an additive $g$ bounded above on some interval $[p,p+h]$ ($h>0$) is linear. Indeed, for $s\in[0,h]$, $g(s)=g(p+s)-g(p)$ is bounded above, and $g(s)=g(h)-g(h-s)$ is bounded below; so $\varphi(t)=g(t)-\frac{g(h)}h t$ is additive, $h$-periodic and bounded on $[0,h]$, hence bounded on $\mathbb R$; since $\varphi(Nt)=N\varphi(t)$ for all $N$, $\varphi\equiv0$.

So it suffices to show that $f$ is bounded above on some interval in $(0,\infty)$.
- If $f(b)\le1$ for all $b\in(0,\frac1{10})$, we are done.
- Otherwise pick $b\in(0,\frac1{10})$ with $f(b)>1$. $E(1,b,x)$ reads
$$f(b^2+bx^2+x)=f(x^2+b^2x+b)+\big(f(b)-1\big)\big(f(x)-f(b)\big)\big(f(x)-1\big).$$
Here $x^2+b^2x+b>0$ (discriminant $b^4-4b<0$), so the first term on the right is positive, and $(t-1)(t-f(b))\ge-\frac{(f(b)-1)^2}4$ for every real $t$. So $f(u)\ge-M$ with $M=\frac{(f(b)-1)^3}4$ for every value $u=bx^2+x+b^2$, i.e. for all $u\ge b^2-\frac1{4b}$. By oddness $f(u)\le M$ for $0<u\le\frac1{4b}-b^2$, an interval since $\frac1{4b}>b^2$.

Hence $f(x)=x^\tau$ for $x>0$. In the second case $f(b)=b^\tau>1$ with $b<1$ would force $\tau<0$, but then $x^\tau$ is unbounded near $0$, contradicting the bound; so the first case holds, $x^\tau\le1$ near $0$ and $\tau\ge0$; $\tau\ne0$ by injectivity. Thus $\tau>0$.

**Step 5: $\tau\in\{1,3\}$.** Take distinct reals $u,v,w$, a small $h>0$ and $a=1+uh$, $b=1+vh$, $c=1+wh$ (all positive). By the mean value theorem, $a^\tau-b^\tau=\tau\eta^{\tau-1}(a-b)$ with $\eta\to1$, so the left side of $E(a,b,c)$ is $\tau^3(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)(1+o(1))$. On the right, $P^\tau-Q^\tau=\tau\xi^{\tau-1}(P-Q)$ with $\xi$ between $P$ and $Q$, both tending to $3$; and $P-Q=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)\ne0$. Dividing by $(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$ and letting $h\to0$:
$$\tau^3=\tau\cdot3^{\tau-1}\iff F(\tau):=3^{(\tau-1)/2}-\tau=0.$$
$F$ is strictly convex, so it has at most two zeros; $F(1)=F(3)=0$. Hence $\tau\in\{1,3\}$, and by oddness $f(x)=x$ or $f(x)=x^3$ for all $x$.

**Conclusion.** Undoing the normalisations ($f\mapsto\pm f$, adding a constant) and including the case $f\equiv$ const, the solutions are
$$f(x)=\alpha x+\beta\quad\text{or}\quad f(x)=\alpha x^3+\beta,\qquad\alpha\in\{-1,0,1\},\ \beta\in\mathbb R.$$
∎

imo-isl-2021-c1.title: Pigeonhole on divisors
imo-isl-2021-c1.body:
**Step 1: a good vertex.** There is $\alpha\in S$ such that the numbers $\gcd(\alpha,s)$, $s\in S\setminus\{\alpha\}$, take at least two values. Otherwise for each $u\in S$ the value $\gcd(u,s)$ would be the same number $g(u)$ for all $s\ne u$, and then
$$\gcd(a,b)=g(a)=\gcd(a,c)=g(c)=\gcd(c,d),$$
contradicting the hypothesis.

**Step 2: an infinite class.** Each $\gcd(\alpha,s)$ is a divisor of $\alpha$, and $\alpha$ has finitely many divisors, while $S\setminus\{\alpha\}$ is infinite. So some divisor $d$ of $\alpha$ has an infinite class
$$B=\{\beta\in S\setminus\{\alpha\}:\gcd(\alpha,\beta)=d\}.$$
By Step 1 there is $\gamma\in S\setminus\{\alpha\}$ with $\gcd(\alpha,\gamma)\ne d$; in particular $\gamma\notin B$.

**Step 3: two elements of $B$ that look the same from $\gamma$.** The values $\gcd(\beta,\gamma)$, $\beta\in B$, are divisors of $\gamma$, so there are distinct $\beta_1,\beta_2\in B$ with $\gcd(\beta_1,\gamma)=\gcd(\beta_2,\gamma)=:d'$. The elements $\alpha,\gamma,\beta_1,\beta_2$ are pairwise distinct.

**Step 4: cases.**
- If $d'=d$: take $(x,y,z)=(\alpha,\beta_1,\gamma)$. Then $\gcd(\alpha,\beta_1)=d=\gcd(\beta_1,\gamma)$ and $\gcd(\gamma,\alpha)\ne d$.
- If $d'\ne d$ and $\gcd(\beta_1,\beta_2)\ne d$: take $(x,y,z)=(\beta_1,\alpha,\beta_2)$; then $\gcd(\beta_1,\alpha)=d=\gcd(\alpha,\beta_2)\ne\gcd(\beta_2,\beta_1)$.
- If $d'\ne d$ and $\gcd(\beta_1,\beta_2)=d$: take $(x,y,z)=(\beta_1,\gamma,\beta_2)$; then $\gcd(\beta_1,\gamma)=d'=\gcd(\gamma,\beta_2)\ne d=\gcd(\beta_2,\beta_1)$.

In every case we found the required triple. ∎

*Graph view.* Colour each edge $\{s,t\}$ of the complete graph on $S$ by $\gcd(s,t)$; every vertex sees finitely many colours, at least two colours occur, and the argument finds a triangle with exactly two colours.

imo-isl-2021-c2.title: A pigeonhole bound and blocks $[1,\dots,n]$ / $[1,1,2,\dots,n]$
imo-isl-2021-c2.body:
By definition the numbers $1,\dots,n$ are not $n$-colourful; we show that $n^2-n-1$ is not $n$-colourful while every $m\ge n^2-n$ is. Note $n^2-n-1\ge n+1$ for $n\ge3$. This proves finiteness and gives the answer.

**$m=n^2-n-1$ is not colourful.** Suppose such a circle exists. If every colour occurred at least $n-1$ times, there would be at least $n(n-1)>m$ marbles; so some colour, say blue, occurs at most $n-2$ times (and at least once, because any $n+1$ consecutive marbles contain blue). The blue marbles cut the circle into at most $n-2$ arcs of consecutive non-blue marbles, containing altogether at least $m-(n-2)=(n-1)^2$ marbles. Since $(n-1)^2=n(n-2)+1>n(n-2)$, some arc contains at least $n+1$ marbles. These are $n+1$ consecutive marbles without blue — a contradiction.

**Every $m\ge n(n-1)$ is colourful.** Write $m=nk+j$ with $0\le j\le n-1$; then $k\ge n-1\ge j$. Around the circle place $k-j$ *short blocks* $[1,2,\dots,n]$ followed by $j$ *long blocks* $[1,1,2,\dots,n]$ (numbers denote colours). This uses $n(k-j)+(n+1)j=m$ marbles.

It suffices to show that for each colour $c$, any two cyclically consecutive marbles of colour $c$ are at distance at most $n+1$ (so at most $n$ marbles lie strictly between them), because then every $n+1$ consecutive marbles contain colour $c$.
- *Colour $c\ge2$* occurs once per block, at offset $c-1$ in a short block and $c$ in a long block (offsets counted from $0$). From its occurrence in a block of length $L$ at offset $o$ to the next block's occurrence at offset $o'$ the distance is $L-o+o'$. For a short block this is $n-(c-1)+o'\in\{n,n+1\}$; for a long block $(n+1)-c+o'\in\{n,n+1\}$.
- *Colour $1$* occurs at offset $0$ of every block and also at offset $1$ of long blocks. The distance from the last $1$ of a block to the first $1$ of the next block is $n$ in both cases, and inside a long block the two $1$'s are adjacent.

So all distances are at most $n+1$ and the arrangement works.

**Answer: the non-colourful numbers are finite in number, and the largest is $n^2-n-1$.** ∎

imo-isl-2021-c4.title: Menger's theorem and swapping $A,B$ in a cut
imo-isl-2021-c4.body:
Model the kingdom as a tournament (a directed graph with exactly one arc between any two vertices). Let $a$ and $b$ be the out-degrees of $A$ and $B$. We prove the stronger statement
$$N_{BA}-N_{AB}=b-a,$$
which immediately gives $N_{AB}=N_{BA}\iff a=b$.

**Tool (Menger's theorem, edge version).** For distinct vertices $s,t$ of a finite directed graph, the maximal number of pairwise arc-disjoint directed paths from $s$ to $t$ equals the minimal size of an $(s,t)$-cut, where an $(s,t)$-cut is a partition $V=S\sqcup T$ with $s\in S$, $t\in T$, and its size $e(S,T)$ is the number of arcs from $S$ to $T$. (Arc-disjoint walks can be shortened to paths by deleting cycles, so it does not matter whether repeated cities are allowed.) Thus $N_{AB}$ is the minimum size of an $(A,B)$-cut and $N_{BA}$ the minimum size of a $(B,A)$-cut.

**Key computation.** Let $(S_A,T_A)$ be any $(A,B)$-cut and define the $(B,A)$-cut
$$S_B=(S_A\setminus\{A\})\cup\{B\},\qquad T_B=(T_A\setminus\{B\})\cup\{A\}.$$
Put $S'=S_A\setminus\{A\}=S_B\setminus\{B\}$ and $T'=T_A\setminus\{B\}=T_B\setminus\{A\}$. Let
- $c$ = number of arcs from $S'$ to $T'$;
- $a_s$, $a_t$ = numbers of arcs from $A$ to $S'$ and from $A$ to $T'\cup\{B\}$ (so $a_s+a_t=a$);
- $b_s$, $b_t$ = numbers of arcs from $B$ to $S'$ and from $B$ to $T'\cup\{A\}$ (so $b_s+b_t=b$).

The arcs from $S_A$ to $T_A$ are: the $c$ arcs $S'\to T'$, the $a_t$ arcs leaving $A$ into $T_A$, and the arcs from $S'$ to $B$; between $B$ and each vertex of $S'$ there is exactly one arc, so there are $|S'|-b_s$ arcs from $S'$ to $B$. Hence
$$e(S_A,T_A)=c+a_t+|S'|-b_s,$$
and symmetrically
$$e(S_B,T_B)=c+b_t+|S'|-a_s.$$
Subtracting, $e(S_B,T_B)-e(S_A,T_A)=(b_t+b_s)-(a_t+a_s)=b-a$.

**Conclusion.** Applying this to a minimum $(A,B)$-cut gives a $(B,A)$-cut of size $N_{AB}+b-a$, so $N_{BA}\le N_{AB}+(b-a)$. Exchanging the roles of $A$ and $B$ gives $N_{AB}\le N_{BA}+(a-b)$. Therefore $N_{BA}-N_{AB}=b-a$, and $N_{AB}=N_{BA}$ holds exactly when $a=b$. ∎

imo-isl-2021-c5.title: Encode the circle and use a gas-station argument
imo-isl-2021-c5.body:
Number the students $1,\dots,2n+1$ around the circle, let $a_i=1$ for a girl and $a_i=0$ for a boy, and extend periodically: $a_{i+2n+1}=a_i$ for all $i\in\mathbb Z$. Since $2k<2n+1$, the $2k$ neighbours of student $i$ are the distinct students $i-k,\dots,i-1,i+1,\dots,i+k$.

Define $b_i=a_i+a_{i-k-1}-1\in\{-1,0,1\}$. Any $2n+1$ consecutive $a$'s sum to $n+1$, hence
$$b_{m+1}+b_{m+2}+\dots+b_{m+2n+1}=(n+1)+(n+1)-(2n+1)=1\qquad(m\in\mathbb Z).\tag{1}$$

**What we need.** Suppose $b_i=1$ and $b_{i+1}+\dots+b_{i+k}\ge0$. Then $a_i=1$ and
$$0\le\sum_{j=1}^k b_{i+j}=\sum_{j=1}^k a_{i+j}+\sum_{j=1}^k a_{i+j-k-1}-k=(a_{i+1}+\dots+a_{i+k})+(a_{i-k}+\dots+a_{i-1})-k,$$
so girl $i$ has at least $k$ girls among her neighbours.

**Such an $i$ exists.** Assume the contrary: whenever $b_i=1$, the sum $b_{i+1}+\dots+b_{i+k}$ is negative. By (1) every block of $2n+1$ consecutive indices contains some $i$ with $b_i=1$. Start with such an $i_0$ and define recursively $i_{j+1}$ = the smallest index $>i_j+k$ with $b_{i_{j+1}}=1$. Among $i_0,\dots,i_{2n+1}$ two are congruent modulo $2n+1$, say $i_p\equiv i_q$ with $p<q$.

For each $j$ consider $S_j=b_{i_j}+b_{i_j+1}+\dots+b_{i_{j+1}-1}$. Its first term is $1$, the next $k$ terms have negative (so $\le-1$) sum by assumption, and the remaining terms $b_t$ with $i_j+k<t<i_{j+1}$ are not equal to $1$ by minimality of $i_{j+1}$, so they are $\le0$. Thus $S_j\le0$.

On the other hand $S_p+\dots+S_{q-1}=\sum_{t=i_p}^{i_q-1}b_t$ is a sum over $i_q-i_p$ consecutive indices, a positive multiple of $2n+1$; splitting it into blocks of length $2n+1$ and using (1), it equals $\frac{i_q-i_p}{2n+1}>0$. This contradicts $S_j\le0$ for all $j$.

Hence the required girl exists. ∎

imo-isl-2021-c6.title: A product of five colourings
imo-isl-2021-c6.body:
**Answer: yes.** Several colourings can be merged into one *product colouring*: a cell gets the tuple of its colours in all of them. The number of colours stays finite, and everything the hunter could read off from any single colouring he can read off from the product. Use coordinates $(x,y)$ for cells and let the rabbit visit $P_0,P_1,P_2,\dots$.

**Colourings $C_1$, $C_2$: tracking moves.** $C_1$ colours a cell by $x\bmod3$, $C_2$ by $y\bmod3$. A move changes exactly one coordinate by $\pm1$; from the colours of $P_t$ and $P_{t+1}$ the hunter sees whether $x\bmod3$ went up, down or stayed, and likewise for $y$. So he knows every move, hence every displacement $P_t-P_0$.

**A marking set.** Let $E=\{k(k+1):k\ge0\}\cup\{-m(m+2):m\ge1\}=\{\dots,-8,-3,0,2,6,12,\dots\}$. Listed in increasing order, the gaps between neighbours are $2,4,6,\dots$ to the right of $0$ and $3,5,7,\dots$ to the left; all gaps are pairwise distinct, and $E$ is unbounded in both directions.

**Colourings $C_3,C_4,C_5$.** $C_3$ colours a cell black if $x\in E$ and white otherwise; $C_4$ does the same with $y$, and $C_5$ with $x+y$.

**Claim.** If the rabbit's $x$-coordinate is unbounded, the hunter can determine $x_0$ at some finite time (similarly for $y$ with $C_4$ and for $x+y$ with $C_5$; each of $x$, $y$, $x+y$ changes by at most $1$ per move, and the hunter knows all their changes).

*Test.* The hunter looks for times $s<t$ such that the $C_3$-reports at $s$ and $t$ are black, $x_t\ne x_s$ (he knows $x_t-x_s$), and all $C_3$-reports at times strictly between $s$ and $t$ are white. Because $x$ changes by at most $1$ per minute, every integer strictly between $x_s$ and $x_t$ is visited at some time in $(s,t)$; all those reports are white, so $x_s$ and $x_t$ are *neighbouring* elements of $E$ with gap $|x_t-x_s|$. Gaps are distinct, so this gap identifies the pair, hence $x_s$, hence $x_0=x_s-(x_s-x_0)$. So whenever the test succeeds, the hunter's deduction is correct.

*The test succeeds.* Say $x$ is unbounded above (below is symmetric). Then the rabbit eventually reaches some $e\in E$ greater than $x_0$, at a time $s_0$, and later reaches the next element $e'$ of $E$ (it must pass it to go higher). Let $t$ be the first time after $s_0$ with $x_t=e'$, and $s$ the last time in $[s_0,t]$ with $x_s=e$. Between $s$ and $t$ the coordinate $x$ never equals $e$ or $e'$, and moving in steps of at most $1$ it stays strictly between them; so the reports are white there, and $(s,t)$ passes the test.

**Two of the three quantities are unbounded.** If the rabbit never gets stuck, it visits infinitely many distinct cells, so $x$ and $y$ cannot both be bounded. If exactly one of $x,y$ is bounded, then $x+y$ is unbounded. So at least two of $x,\ y,\ x+y$ are unbounded, and after finite time the hunter knows two of $x_0,\ y_0,\ x_0+y_0$, hence all three, i.e. the starting cell.

So with the product colouring $C_1\times C_2\times C_3\times C_4\times C_5$ (72 colours) the hunter wins: either the rabbit gets stuck, or after finitely many minutes he determines the starting cell. ∎

imo-isl-2021-c7.title: Explicit construction; counting hops from red and blue cells

imo-isl-2021-c8.title: Patterns of pairs $\{2k-1,2k\}$ and parity constraints
imo-isl-2021-c8.body:
**Upper bound.** In a row, replace both $2k-1$ and $2k$ by a symbol $x_k$ ($k=1,\dots,50$). The result, the *pattern* of the row, is an arrangement of $x_1,\dots,x_{50}$ in which each symbol occurs twice; there are $\frac{100!}{2^{50}}$ patterns. If two rows had the same pattern, then in every column their entries would be $2k-1$ and $2k$ in some order or equal, so they would differ by at most $1$ everywhere, violating (ii). Hence distinct rows have distinct patterns and $N\le\frac{100!}{2^{50}}$.

**Construction.** For a row (a permutation) and a set $G$ of values, read the elements of $G$ from left to right; this word is a permutation of $G$ and has a parity. Take as rows *all* permutations of $1,\dots,100$ for which each of the 50 sets
$$G_1=\{1,2\},\ G_2=\{2,3,4\},\ G_3=\{4,5,6\},\ \dots,\ G_{50}=\{98,99,100\}$$
is read in an *even* order.

*Counting.* Each pattern gives exactly one such row: put $1,2$ in the places of $x_1$ with $1$ first; then for $k=2,\dots,50$ the place of $2k-2$ is already fixed, and of the two ways to put $2k-1,2k$ into the places of $x_k$, exactly one makes $G_k$ even (exchanging $2k-1$ and $2k$ is a transposition and flips the parity). So there are exactly $\frac{100!}{2^{50}}$ rows, all distinct, and (i) holds.

*Property (ii).* Suppose two distinct rows $\pi_1,\pi_2$ have $|\pi_1(c)-\pi_2(c)|\le1$ in every column $c$. Let $\sigma$ be the permutation of values with $\sigma(\pi_1(c))=\pi_2(c)$; then $|\sigma(v)-v|\le1$ for all $v$.

*Lemma.* A permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with $|\sigma(v)-v|\le1$ for all $v$ is a product of disjoint transpositions of the form $(v\ v{+}1)$. *Proof by induction on $n$:* $\sigma(n)\in\{n-1,n\}$. If $\sigma(n)=n$, restrict to $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$. Otherwise $\sigma(n)=n-1$, and the value $u$ with $\sigma(u)=n$ satisfies $u\ge n-1$, $u\ne n$, so $u=n-1$: $\sigma$ swaps $n-1,n$; restrict to $\{1,\dots,n-2\}$. $\square$

So $\pi_2$ arises from $\pi_1$ by exchanging the positions of $v$ and $v+1$ for all $v$ in a non-empty set $D$ of pairwise non-adjacent numbers. Let $r=\min D$.
- If $r=2k-1$ is odd: in $G_k$ (or $G_1$ when $k=1$) the values $2k-1,2k$ exchange places, while $2k-2$ does not move (its possible swaps would need an element of $D$ smaller than $r$). So the word of $G_k$ changes by a transposition and its parity flips — impossible, as both rows are even on $G_k$.
- If $r=2k$ is even: in $G_{k+1}=\{2k,2k+1,2k+2\}$ the values $2k,2k+1$ exchange places. If $2k+2$ did not move, the parity of $G_{k+1}$ would flip; and $2k+2$ can move only via $2k+2\in D$ ($2k+1\notin D$ since $D$ has no adjacent elements). Hence $2k+2\in D$. Repeating the argument with $G_{k+2},G_{k+3},\dots$ gives $2k+4,\dots,98\in D$. But then in $G_{50}=\{98,99,100\}$ the values $98,99$ swap while $100$ stays (there is no $101$), and the parity flips — a contradiction.

So the table satisfies (ii), and the maximum is
$$N=\frac{100!}{2^{50}}.$$
∎

imo-isl-2021-g1.title: Two auxiliary circles (directed angles)
imo-isl-2021-g1.body:
We use directed angles $\measuredangle(\ell,m)$ between lines, taken modulo $180^\circ$.

**Preliminaries.** In the parallelogram $AD=BC=AC$. So triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $CA=CB$ and triangle $ACD$ is isosceles with $AC=AD$; together with $AB\parallel CD$ this gives
$$\measuredangle(BC,BA)=\measuredangle(AB,AC)=\measuredangle(CD,CA)=\measuredangle(DA,DC).\tag{1}$$
(The first equality is the base angles of $CA=CB$, the second uses $AB\parallel CD$, the third is the base angles of $AC=AD$.)

**Step 1: $A,B,C,R$ are concyclic (circle $\gamma$).** Using that $C,R,P$ are collinear, $APRQ$ is cyclic, $D,Q,P$ are collinear and $AQCD$ is cyclic:
$$\measuredangle(RC,RA)=\measuredangle(RP,RA)=\measuredangle(QP,QA)=\measuredangle(QD,QA)=\measuredangle(CD,CA)\overset{(1)}=\measuredangle(BC,BA).$$
Hence $R$ lies on the circle $ABC$.

**Step 2: $C,Q,R,X$ are concyclic (circle $\delta$),** where $X=AQ\cap CD$. Using circle $APRQ$ and then $PR=CR$ (same line) and $PA=AB\parallel CD=CX$:
$$\measuredangle(QR,QX)=\measuredangle(QR,QA)=\measuredangle(PR,PA)=\measuredangle(CR,CX).$$

**Step 3: $B,R,X$ are collinear.** Using $\delta$, then $QX=QA$ and circle $AQCD$, then (1), then $\gamma$:
$$\measuredangle(RX,RC)=\measuredangle(QX,QC)=\measuredangle(QA,QC)=\measuredangle(DA,DC)=\measuredangle(AB,AC)=\measuredangle(RB,RC).$$
So the lines $RX$ and $RB$ make the same angle with $RC$, hence coincide: $X$ lies on $BR$.

Therefore $BR$ passes through $X=AQ\cap CD$, i.e. the three lines are concurrent. ∎

imo-isl-2021-g1.title: Tangent line and Pascal
imo-isl-2021-g1.body:
Let $\alpha$ be the circle $APRQ$ and use the notation of the first solution (for the configuration of the figure). We have $\angle CAP=\angle ACD=\angle AQD=180^\circ-\angle AQP$ (alternate angles, circle $AQCD$, and $D,Q,P$ collinear), so by the converse of the tangent–chord theorem the line $AC$ is tangent to $\alpha$ at $A$.

Let $AD$ meet $\alpha$ again at $Y$. Using the tangency of $AC$ to $\alpha$, the parallel $AD\parallel BC$ and the circle $\gamma=ABCR$ from the first solution, $\angle ARY=\angle CAD=\angle ACB=\angle ARB$, so $Y,B,R$ are collinear.

Apply Pascal's theorem to the hexagon $AAYRPQ$ inscribed in $\alpha$ (the side $AA$ is the tangent at $A$, i.e. the line $AC$): the points $AA\cap RP=C$, $AY\cap PQ=D$ and $YR\cap QA$ are collinear. So $YR=BR$ meets $AQ$ on the line $CD$, which is the claim. ∎

imo-isl-2021-g3.title: Area bounded by squared distances to the centre
imo-isl-2021-g3.body:
Let $O=\left(n-\frac12,n-\frac12\right)$ be the centre of $S$, and write $[\,\cdot\,]$ for area.

**Lemma.** For any polygon $A_1A_2\dots A_m$ and any point $O$,
$$[A_1\dots A_m]\le\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m OA_i^2,$$
with equality if the polygon is a square centred at $O$.

*Proof.* By the shoelace formula the area is the absolute value of the sum of the signed areas of the triangles $OA_iA_{i+1}$ ($A_{m+1}=A_1$), so
$$[A_1\dots A_m]\le\sum_{i=1}^m[OA_iA_{i+1}]\le\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{OA_i\cdot OA_{i+1}}2\le\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{OA_i^2+OA_{i+1}^2}4=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m OA_i^2.$$
For a square centred at $O$ the four triangles are right isosceles with legs $OA_i=OA_{i+1}$ and do not overlap, so every inequality is an equality. $\square$

**Upper bound.** Summing the lemma over the quadrilaterals of $\mathcal F$, and using that every point of $S$ is a vertex of exactly one of them,
$$\Sigma(\mathcal F)\le\frac12\sum_{A\in S}OA^2.$$

**Computing the bound.** 
$$\sum_{A\in S}OA^2=\sum_{i=0}^{2n-1}\sum_{j=0}^{2n-1}\left[\left(i-n+\tfrac12\right)^2+\left(j-n+\tfrac12\right)^2\right]=2\cdot2n\sum_{i=0}^{2n-1}\left(i-n+\tfrac12\right)^2.$$
The numbers $i-n+\frac12$ are $\pm\frac12,\pm\frac32,\dots,\pm\frac{2n-1}2$, so
$$\sum_{i=0}^{2n-1}\left(i-n+\tfrac12\right)^2=\frac12\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}(2t+1)^2=\frac12\cdot\frac{n(2n-1)(2n+1)}3.$$
Hence $\frac12\sum_{A\in S}OA^2=\frac13n^2(2n-1)(2n+1)$.

**Equality.** The rotation by $90^\circ$ about $O$ maps $S$ onto itself, and $O$ is not a lattice point, so each $A\in S$ together with its three rotated images forms a square centred at $O$ with vertices in $S$. These $4n^2/4=n^2$ *central squares* partition $S$, so they form an admissible family $\mathcal F$, and by the equality case of the lemma their total area is exactly $\frac13n^2(2n-1)(2n+1)$.

**Answer: $\frac13n^2(2n+1)(2n-1)$.** ∎

*Remark.* The same proof works verbatim if $\mathcal F$ may consist of arbitrary polygons (each point of $S$ a vertex of exactly one of them): the maximum is the same.

imo-isl-2021-g3.title: Diagonals and a rearrangement bound (quadrilaterals only)
imo-isl-2021-g3.body:
For a quadrilateral $ABCD$ with diagonals meeting at angle $\varphi$, $[ABCD]=\frac12AC\cdot BD\sin\varphi\le\frac14(AC^2+BD^2)$ (this also holds for non-convex quadrilaterals, where the area is at most $\frac12AC\cdot BD$). Summing, $\Sigma(\mathcal F)\le\frac14\sum_{i=1}^{2n^2}A_iB_i^2$, where the $4n^2$ points $A_i,B_i$ are all of $S$, paired along the diagonals.

With $A_i=(p_i,q_i)$, $B_i=(r_i,s_i)$: $\sum(p_i-r_i)^2=\sum\big(2p_i^2+2r_i^2-(p_i+r_i)^2\big)$. The first part equals $4n\sum_{j=0}^{2n-1}j^2$ (each $x$-coordinate occurs $2n$ times), and by QM–AM $\sum(p_i+r_i)^2\ge\frac1{2n^2}\big(\sum(p_i+r_i)\big)^2=\frac1{2n^2}\big(2n\cdot n(2n-1)\big)^2$. This gives $\sum(p_i-r_i)^2\le\frac{2n^2(2n-1)(2n+1)}3$, and the same for the $y$-coordinates. Hence $\Sigma(\mathcal F)\le\frac14\cdot\frac{4n^2(4n^2-1)}3=\frac13n^2(2n-1)(2n+1)$, attained by the central squares. ∎

imo-isl-2021-g4.title: Two tangent circles and a homothety (directed angles)
imo-isl-2021-g4.body:
Directed angles $\measuredangle(\ell,m)$ are taken mod $180^\circ$; $t$ denotes the tangent line $EF$ to $\Omega$ at $D$. Let $TE$ and $TF$ meet $AC$ at $P$ and $Q$.

**Step 1: $A,P,D,E$ concyclic ($\alpha$) and $C,Q,D,F$ concyclic ($\gamma$).** By $PE\parallel CD$ and the tangent–chord theorem in $\Omega$,
$$\measuredangle(PE,PA)=\measuredangle(CD,CA)=\measuredangle(DE,DA),$$
so $P\in(ADE)$. Similarly $\measuredangle(QF,QC)=\measuredangle(AD,AC)=\measuredangle(DF,DC)$, so $Q\in(CDF)$.

**Step 2: $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ are tangent at $D$.** Let $\ell$, $\ell'$ be their tangents at $D$. By the tangent–chord theorem, $\measuredangle(\ell,DA)=\measuredangle(ED,EA)=\measuredangle(t,AB)$ and $\measuredangle(\ell',DC)=\measuredangle(FD,FC)=\measuredangle(t,BC)$. Hence
$$\measuredangle(\ell,\ell')=\measuredangle(t,AB)+\measuredangle(DA,DC)-\measuredangle(t,BC)=\measuredangle(BC,BA)+\measuredangle(DA,DC)=0,$$
because $ABCD$ is cyclic. So $\ell=\ell'$.

**Step 3: $DT$ is the common tangent.** We have $\measuredangle(FQ,FE)=\measuredangle(AD,t)$ (as $FQ=FT\parallel AD$) and $\measuredangle(PQ,PE)=\measuredangle(PA,PE)=\measuredangle(DA,DE)=\measuredangle(AD,t)$ (circle $\alpha$). So $P,Q,E,F$ are concyclic and $TP\cdot TE=TQ\cdot TF$ (signed). Thus $T$ has equal powers with respect to $\alpha$ and $\gamma$, i.e. $T$ lies on their radical axis, which is the common tangent $\ell$ at $D$. So $DT=\ell$.

**Step 4: $TK\parallel BD$.** As $TD=TK$ and $K\in t$, $\measuredangle(KT,KD)=\measuredangle(DK,DT)=\measuredangle(DE,DT)$. Since $DT$ is tangent to $\alpha$, $\measuredangle(DE,DT)=\measuredangle(AE,AD)=\measuredangle(AB,AD)$, and by the tangent–chord theorem in $\Omega$, $\measuredangle(AB,AD)=\measuredangle(DB,t)$. So $\measuredangle(KT,t)=\measuredangle(DB,t)$, i.e. $KT\parallel DB$. In the same way, as $DT$ is also tangent to $\gamma$: $\measuredangle(KT,KD)=\measuredangle(DF,DT)=\measuredangle(CF,CD)$.

**Step 5: $T,P,Q,D,K$ lie on one circle $\tau$.** From Step 4, $\measuredangle(KT,KD)=\measuredangle(AE,AD)=\measuredangle(PE,PD)=\measuredangle(PT,PD)$ (circle $\alpha$), so $P\in(TDK)$. Likewise $\measuredangle(KT,KD)=\measuredangle(CF,CD)=\measuredangle(QF,QD)=\measuredangle(QT,QD)$ (circle $\gamma$), so $Q\in(TDK)$.

**Step 6: $PK\parallel BC$.** $\measuredangle(KP,KD)=\measuredangle(QP,QD)=\measuredangle(QC,QD)=\measuredangle(FC,FD)$ by $\tau$ and $\gamma$; so $\measuredangle(KP,t)=\measuredangle(BC,t)$ and $KP\parallel BC$.

**Step 7: conclusion.** The triangles $TPK$ and $DCB$ have pairwise parallel sides: $TP\parallel DC$, $PK\parallel CB$, $KT\parallel BD$. Hence they are homothetic or differ by a translation. A translation is impossible: it would move $P\in AC$ to $C$, i.e. be a translation along $AC$, and keep $T$ on its side of line $AC$; but $T$ (inside triangle $ABC$) and $D$ lie on opposite sides of $AC$. So there is a homothety mapping $T\mapsto D$, $P\mapsto C$, $K\mapsto B$, and the lines $TD$, $PC=AC$ and $KB$ pass through its centre. ∎

imo-isl-2021-g5.title: Radical axes and coordinates on $AC$
imo-isl-2021-g5.body:
Let $\Omega$ be the circle $ABCD$, $\gamma_B$ and $\gamma_D$ the circles with centres $O_B$, $O_D$. Write $a=AB$, $b=BC$, $c=CD$, $d=DA$ (pairwise different) and $H=AC\cap BD$, which lies inside both diagonals.

**Step 1: reduction to radical axes.** $\gamma_B\ne\Omega$ (it is tangent to $AC$, $\Omega$ is not), so the radical axis $\ell_B$ of $\Omega,\gamma_B$ is a line through their common point $B$, perpendicular to $OO_B$. Likewise $\ell_D$ passes through $D$ and is perpendicular to $OO_D$. Hence
$$O\in O_BO_D\iff OO_B\parallel OO_D\iff \ell_B\parallel\ell_D.$$

**Step 2: identifying the radical axes.** Since $a\ne b$, the tangent to $\Omega$ at $B$ is not parallel to $AC$; let it meet line $AC$ at $L_B$. Using directed angles, the tangent–chord theorem and $\measuredangle(BC,BB_1)=\measuredangle(BB_1,BA)$ (bisector):
$$\measuredangle(BL_B,BB_1)=\measuredangle(BL_B,BC)+\measuredangle(BC,BB_1)=\measuredangle(AB,AC)+\measuredangle(BB_1,BA)=\measuredangle(B_1B,B_1L_B).$$
So triangle $L_BBB_1$ is isosceles with $L_BB=L_BB_1$. The power of $L_B$ with respect to $\Omega$ is $L_BB^2$, and with respect to $\gamma_D$ (tangent to line $AC$ at $B_1$) it is $L_BB_1^2$. These are equal, so $L_B\in\ell_D$, and $\ell_D=DL_B$. Similarly, with $L_D$ the intersection of the tangent at $D$ with $AC$ (exists as $c\ne d$), $\ell_B=BL_D$. We must show $BL_D\parallel DL_B$.

**Step 3: coordinates on $AC$.** Put a coordinate on line $AC$ with $A=0$, $C=1$ (so lengths along $AC$ are measured in units of $AC$).
- By the angle bisector theorem, $B_1=\frac a{a+b}$ and $D_1=\frac d{c+d}$.
- Triangles $ABD$ and $CBD$ share the base $BD$, and $\sin\angle BAD=\sin\angle BCD$; so $\frac{AH}{HC}=\frac{[ABD]}{[CBD]}=\frac{ad}{bc}$ and $H=h:=\frac{ad}{ad+bc}$. Similarly $\frac{HD}{HB}=\frac{[ACD]}{[ACB]}=\frac{cd}{ab}$.
- Triangles $L_BBA$ and $L_BCB$ are similar (common angle at $L_B$, and $\angle L_BBC=\angle BAC$ by tangent–chord), so $\frac{L_BA}{L_BB}=\frac{L_BB}{L_BC}=\frac ab$ and $\frac{L_BA}{L_BC}=\frac{a^2}{b^2}$. $L_B$ is outside $\Omega$, hence outside the segment $AC$, so its coordinate $x$ satisfies $\frac x{x-1}=\frac{a^2}{b^2}$: $L_B=\frac{a^2}{a^2-b^2}$. Likewise $L_D=\frac{d^2}{d^2-c^2}$.

Let $\kappa=-\frac{cd}{ab}$; the homothety $\eta$ with centre $H$ and ratio $\kappa$ maps $B$ to $D$ ($H$ lies between them). Along line $AC$ it acts by $x\mapsto h+\kappa(x-h)$.

**Step 4: the hypothesis.** $BD_1\parallel DB_1$ means $\eta$ maps the line $BD_1$ to the parallel line through $D$, i.e. $\eta(D_1)=B_1$: $B_1-h=\kappa(D_1-h)$. Now
$$B_1-h=\frac a{a+b}-\frac{ad}{ad+bc}=\frac{ab(c-d)}{(a+b)(ad+bc)},\qquad D_1-h=\frac d{c+d}-\frac{ad}{ad+bc}=\frac{cd(b-a)}{(c+d)(ad+bc)},$$
so the hypothesis is equivalent to $\frac{ab(c-d)}{a+b}=\frac{c^2d^2(a-b)}{ab(c+d)}$, i.e.
$$a^2b^2(c^2-d^2)=c^2d^2(a^2-b^2).\tag{$*$}$$

**Step 5: the conclusion.** Similarly
$$L_B-h=\frac{a^2}{a^2-b^2}-\frac{ad}{ad+bc}=\frac{ab(ac+bd)}{(a^2-b^2)(ad+bc)},\qquad L_D-h=\frac{d^2}{d^2-c^2}-\frac{ad}{ad+bc}=\frac{cd(ac+bd)}{(d^2-c^2)(ad+bc)}.$$
Then $L_B-h=\kappa(L_D-h)$ is equivalent to $\frac{ab}{a^2-b^2}=\frac{c^2d^2}{ab(c^2-d^2)}$, which is exactly $(*)$. Hence $\eta(L_D)=L_B$. Since also $\eta(B)=D$, the homothety maps the line $BL_D$ onto the line $DL_B$, so these lines are parallel: $\ell_B\parallel\ell_D$.

By Step 1, $O$ lies on the line $O_BO_D$. ∎

imo-isl-2021-g6.title: Thin counterexamples; the longest diagonal for odd $n$
imo-isl-2021-g6.body:
**Even $n$ fail.** Take a regular $k$-gon $A_0A_1\dots A_{k-1}$ with side $1$, $k$ large, and let $B_i$ be the reflection of $A_i$ in the line $A_0A_{n/2}$. Then $A_0A_1\dots A_{n/2}B_{n/2-1}\dots B_1$ is a convex $n$-gon with unit sides (convex because its angles at $A_0$ and $A_{n/2}$ are small). It lies within distance $h$ of the line $A_0A_{n/2}$, where $h$ is the sagitta of an arc of angle $\frac{\pi n}{k}$ on a circle of radius $\frac1{2\sin(\pi/k)}$; $h\to0$ as $k\to\infty$. So for large $k$ the polygon lies in a strip of width $<\frac{\sqrt3}2$. But a unit equilateral triangle does not fit in such a strip: if a triangle lies in a strip, the line through its "middle" vertex parallel to the strip cuts it into two triangles, so its area is at most $\frac12\cdot w\cdot s$, where $w$ is the strip width and $s\le1$ the length of the cut; area $\frac{\sqrt3}4$ forces $w\ge\frac{\sqrt3}2$.

**Odd $n$ work.** Let $n=2k+1$. For $k=1$ the polygon is itself a unit equilateral triangle, so let $k\ge2$, and let $P$ be a convex $(2k+1)$-gon with unit sides. The average interior angle of $P$ is $\frac{(n-2)\cdot180^\circ}{n}>90^\circ$, so some angle $A_{i-1}A_iA_{i+1}$ is at least $90^\circ$ and the diagonal $A_{i-1}A_{i+1}$ has length at least $\sqrt2$; hence the longest diagonal $d$ has length $>1$. The endpoints of $d$ split the boundary into two polylines with $2k+1$ unit sides in total, so we may label $P=A_0A_1\dots A_{2k}$ with $d=A_0A_\ell$ and $k+1\le\ell\le2k-1$. Let $Q=A_0A_1\dots A_\ell\subseteq P$ (convex).

*Case 1: $\angle A_\ell A_0A_1\ge60^\circ$.* $A_1A_\ell$ is a diagonal, so $A_1A_\ell\le A_0A_\ell$, hence in triangle $A_0A_1A_\ell$ the angle at $A_1$ is at least the angle at $A_0$, so both angles at the side $A_0A_1$ are $\ge60^\circ$. Then the equilateral triangle on $A_0A_1$ on the side of $A_\ell$ lies inside triangle $A_0A_1A_\ell\subseteq P$. The case $\angle A_{\ell-1}A_\ell A_0\ge60^\circ$ is symmetric.

*Case 2: both angles $\angle A_\ell A_0A_1$ and $\angle A_{\ell-1}A_\ell A_0$ are $<60^\circ$.* Then every vertex of $Q$ lies in the region $W$ bounded by the segment $A_0A_\ell$ and the two rays from $A_0$ and $A_\ell$ making $60^\circ$ with it (on the side of $Q$). Let $\mathcal T=A_0YZA_\ell$ be the isosceles trapezoid consisting of the points of $W$ at distance at most $\frac{\sqrt3}2$ from $A_0A_\ell$ (it has $YZ\parallel A_0A_\ell$, legs $A_0Y=A_\ell Z=1$ at $60^\circ$ to the base, and $YZ=A_0A_\ell-1>0$); its perimeter is $2A_0A_\ell+1$.

Suppose $Q\subseteq\mathcal T$. A convex polygon inside another has smaller or equal perimeter, so $\ell+A_0A_\ell\le2A_0A_\ell+1$, i.e. $\ell-1\le A_0A_\ell$. But by the triangle inequality along the other polyline (at least two sides, not collinear), $A_0A_\ell<2k+1-\ell\le\ell-1$. Contradiction.

So some vertex $A_m$ of $Q$ lies in $W$ but outside $\mathcal T$; its distance to $A_0A_\ell$ is greater than $\frac{\sqrt3}2$. Let $M$ be its projection on $A_0A_\ell$. As $\angle A_mA_0A_\ell<60^\circ$, $A_0M=MA_m\cot\angle A_mA_0M>\frac{\sqrt3}2\cdot\frac1{\sqrt3}=\frac12$, and likewise $MA_\ell>\frac12$. Choose $U,V$ on $A_0A_\ell$ with $MU=MV=\frac12$ on either side of $M$, and $N$ on $MA_m$ with $MN=\frac{\sqrt3}2$. Then $UVN$ is a unit equilateral triangle inside triangle $A_0A_mA_\ell\subseteq P$.

**Answer: exactly the odd $n\ge3$.** ∎

imo-isl-2021-g8.title: Brianchon's theorem and right angles (directed angles)
imo-isl-2021-g8.body:
Directed angles $\measuredangle(\ell,m)$ are mod $180^\circ$. Let $D$ be the tangency point of $BC$ with $\Omega_A$ and $D'$ the antipode of $D$ on $\Omega_A$, so the tangent $t'$ to $\Omega_A$ at $D'$ is parallel to $BC$. Let $R'$ be the point of $t'$ with $AR'\perp BC$. We show that $PR'$ is tangent to the circle $APX$; by the same argument with $Y,Q$ in place of $X,P$, $QR'$ is tangent to the circle $AQY$, hence $R=R'$ and $AR\perp BC$.

Let the tangent to $\Omega_A$ at $X$ (the line $PX$) meet $AB$ at $S$ and $t'$ at $T$, and let $U$ be the common point at infinity of the parallel lines $BC$ and $t'$.

**Step 1: a point $V$ with $SV\parallel BC$.** The (degenerate) hexagon $ASXTUC$ is circumscribed about $\Omega_A$: its sides lie on the lines $AB$, the tangent at $X$ (twice, $X$ being its point of contact), $t'$, $BC$ and $CA$, all tangent to $\Omega_A$. By Brianchon's theorem its main diagonals $AT$, $SU$, $XC$ are concurrent at a point $V$. As $SU$ is the line through $S$ parallel to $BC$, we get $SV\parallel BC$.

**Step 2: $A,X,S,V$ are concyclic.** Using $SV\parallel BC$, $V\in XC$ and the circle $\omega$ through $A,B,C,X$:
$$\measuredangle(VS,VX)=\measuredangle(BC,CX)=\measuredangle(AB,AX)=\measuredangle(AS,AX).$$
Consequently, since $SV\parallel BC\parallel t'=TR'$ and $V\in AT$,
$$\measuredangle(PX,XA)=\measuredangle(XS,XA)=\measuredangle(VS,VA)=\measuredangle(TR',TA).\tag{1}$$

**Step 3: $A,P,R',T$ are concyclic.** $\angle APT=90^\circ$ ($P$ is the foot from $A$ on the line $PX\ni T$) and $\angle AR'T=90^\circ$ ($AR'\perp BC\parallel TR'$), so $P$ and $R'$ lie on the circle with diameter $AT$.

**Step 4: tangency.** In the right triangles $APX$ (right angle at $P$) and $AR'T$ (right angle at $R'$),
$$\measuredangle(XA,AP)=90^\circ-\measuredangle(PX,XA),\qquad\measuredangle(TA,AR')=90^\circ-\measuredangle(R'T,TA).$$
By (1) these are equal, and by Step 3, $\measuredangle(TA,AR')=\measuredangle(TP,PR')=\measuredangle(PX,PR')$. Hence
$$\measuredangle(PX,PR')=\measuredangle(AX,AP).$$
By the converse of the tangent–chord theorem (the tangent $m$ at $P$ to the circle $APX$ is characterised by $\measuredangle(PX,m)=\measuredangle(AX,AP)$), the line $PR'$ is tangent to the circle $APX$ at $P$.

As explained at the start, the same holds for $QR'$ and the circle $AQY$, so the two tangents meet at $R=R'$, and $AR=AR'\perp BC$. ∎

imo-isl-2021-n1.title: Reduce the numerator modulo the denominator
imo-isl-2021-n1.body:
Let $M=a^2+b+3$. Since $b\equiv-a^2-3\pmod M$,
$$ab+3b+8\equiv a(-a^2-3)+3(-a^2-3)+8=-(a^3+3a^2+3a+1)=-(a+1)^3\pmod M.$$
If the fraction equals an integer $n$, then $M\mid ab+3b+8$, so $M\mid(a+1)^3$.

**$M$ divides $(a+1)^2$.** For every prime $p$, $v_p(M)\le2$ (no prime cube divides $M$) and $v_p(M)\le3v_p(a+1)$. If $v_p(a+1)=0$ then $v_p(M)=0$; otherwise $v_p(M)\le2\le2v_p(a+1)$. So $M\mid(a+1)^2$.

**In fact $M=(a+1)^2$.** We have $0<(a+1)^2<2M$, because $2M-(a+1)^2=(a-1)^2+2b+4>0$. A positive multiple of $M$ smaller than $2M$ equals $M$.

So $a^2+b+3=a^2+2a+1$, i.e. $b=2a-2$, and then
$$n=\frac{a(2a-2)+3(2a-2)+8}{(a+1)^2}=\frac{2a^2+4a+2}{(a+1)^2}=2.$$
Conversely $(a,b)=(2,2)$ gives $M=9$ (cube-free) and $\frac{4+6+8}{9}=2$.

**Answer: only $n=2$.** ∎

imo-isl-2021-n3.title: Force $d_i=2i-1$ by induction
imo-isl-2021-n3.body:
Write $d_1+\dots+d_i=s_i^2$ with $s_i\ge1$, and $s_0=0$. Then $0=s_0<s_1<\dots<s_k$, so $s_i\ge i$, and
$$d_i=s_i^2-s_{i-1}^2=(s_i-s_{i-1})(s_i+s_{i-1})\ge s_i+s_{i-1}\ge2i-1.\tag{1}$$

**Claim.** $d_i=2i-1$ and $s_i=i$ for $i=1,\dots,k$.

*Base.* The divisor $1$ equals some $d_j$, and (1) gives $1\ge2j-1$, so $j=1$: $d_1=1=s_1^2$, $s_1=1$.

*Step.* Suppose $d_j=2j-1$, $s_j=j$ for $j\le i<k$. Then $d_{i+1}=s_{i+1}^2-i^2=(s_{i+1}-i)(s_{i+1}+i)$, so $s_{i+1}+i$ divides $d_{i+1}$ and hence $n$; say $s_{i+1}+i=d_j$.
- If $j\ge i+2$: by (1), $d_j\ge s_j+s_{j-1}\ge s_{i+2}+s_{i+1}>s_{i+1}+s_i=s_{i+1}+i$, impossible.
- If $j\le i$: $d_j=2j-1\le2i-1<2i+1\le s_{i+1}+i$, impossible.

So $j=i+1$, i.e. $(s_{i+1}-i)(s_{i+1}+i)=s_{i+1}+i$, which gives $s_{i+1}-i=1$: $s_{i+1}=i+1$ and $d_{i+1}=2i+1$. $\square$

**Conclusion.** The divisors of $n$ are exactly $1,3,5,\dots,2k-1$. The largest is $n=2k-1$. If $k\ge2$, the second largest divisor is $n-2$, and $n-2\mid n$ gives $n-2\mid2$; since $n$ is odd, $n-2=1$, $n=3$. If $k=1$ then $n=1$.

Both work: for $n=1$, $1=1^2$; for $n=3$, $1=1^2$ and $1+3=2^2$.

**Answer: $n=1$ and $n=3$.** ∎

imo-isl-2021-n4.title: Reduce to an equation in powers of $r$; reduce mod $a-b$ and $a+b$
imo-isl-2021-n4.body:
**Setting up.** Put coordinates with the red bead at $0$ and the blue bead at $1$ initially; the goal is to bring the red bead to $1$. A move multiplies the distance between the beads by $r^k>0$ and never changes their order, so the red bead is always to the left and the distance is always a power $r^\ell$, $\ell\in\mathbb Z$. Let $d_m$ be the distance after $m$ moves ($d_0=1$). Every sequence of powers of $r$ can be realised as $d_1,d_2,\dots$ (with either bead moving at each step). If the red bead moves at move $m+1$, its coordinate increases by $d_m-d_{m+1}$; if the blue bead moves, the red one stays.

Two consecutive moves of the same bead can be replaced by one, so we may assume the beads alternate; let the red bead move $t$ times.

- *Red moves first* (moves $1,3,\dots,2t-1$, so $2t-1\le2021$, $t\le1011$): the condition is $\sum_{j=1}^t(d_{2j-2}-d_{2j-1})=1$, i.e. $\sum_{j=1}^{t}d_{2j-1}=\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}d_{2j}$.
- *Blue moves first* (red moves are $2,4,\dots,2t$, so $t\le1010$): the condition is $\sum_{j=1}^t(d_{2j-1}-d_{2j})=1=r^0$, i.e. $\sum_{j=1}^t d_{2j-1}=r^0+\sum_{j=1}^t d_{2j}$.

Both are of the form
$$\sum_{i=1}^{N}r^{\beta_i}=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}r^{\gamma_i}\qquad(\beta_i,\gamma_i\in\mathbb Z)\tag{1}$$
with $N\le1011$ ($N=t$, resp. $N=t+1$). Adding the term $r^0$ to both sides we may take $N=1011$ exactly. Conversely, a solution of (1) with $N=1011$ gives distances $d_{2j-1}=r^{\beta_j}$ ($j\le1011$), $d_{2j}=r^{\gamma_j}$ ($j\le1010$); with red moving at the odd moves $1,3,\dots,2021$ the red bead advances by $1+\sum r^{\gamma_j}-\sum r^{\beta_j}=1$. So **Alice succeeds iff (1) is solvable with $N=1011$** (equivalently with some $N\le1011$).

**Necessity.** Let $r=\frac ab$ in lowest terms, $a>b\ge1$. Shift all exponents by a common integer so that they lie in $\{0,1,\dots,L\}$ and multiply (1) by $b^L$; moving everything to one side gives
$$\sum_{i=1}^{2N-1}\varepsilon_i\,a^{\mu_i}b^{L-\mu_i}=0,\qquad\varepsilon_i=\pm1,\ \ \textstyle\sum\varepsilon_i=1.\tag{2}$$
- Modulo $a-b$ (where $a\equiv b$) the left side is $\equiv b^L\sum\varepsilon_i=b^L$. As $\gcd(a-b,b)=1$, this forces $a-b=1$.
- Modulo $a+b$ (where $a\equiv-b$) the left side is $\equiv b^L\sum\varepsilon_i(-1)^{\mu_i}=:b^LS$, where $S$ is a sum of $2N-1$ terms $\pm1$, hence odd and non-zero, with $|S|\le2N-1$. As $\gcd(a+b,b)=1$, $a+b\mid S$, so $a+b\le2N-1=2021$.

With $a=b+1$: $2b+1\le2021$, so $b\le1010$.

**Sufficiency.** For $r=\frac{b+1}b$ with $b\le1010$, take $N=b+1\le1011$, all $\beta_i=0$ and all $\gamma_i=1$: $(b+1)\cdot1=b\cdot\frac{b+1}{b}$. So (1) is solvable and Alice succeeds.

**Answer: $r=\frac{b+1}b$ for $b=1,2,\dots,1010$.** ∎

imo-isl-2021-n5.title: Size bound, parity, and lifting the exponent
imo-isl-2021-n5.body:
For each fixed $n$ there are finitely many solutions (each of $a,b,c$ is at most $(n!)^{1/(n-1)}$). We show that there is no solution with $n>100$; this proves the claim. So let $n>100$. We use $v_p$ for the $p$-adic valuation and Legendre's bound
$$v_p(n!)=\sum_{s\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac n{p^s}\right\rfloor<\sum_{s\ge1}\frac n{p^s}=\frac n{p-1}.\tag{$\heartsuit$}$$

**Size bound.** $n!=2\cdot\big(3\cdot4\cdots(n-4)\big)\cdot(n-3)(n-2)(n-1)n$. Here $(n-3)n\le(n-1)^2$, so the last four factors give at most $(n-1)^4$, and by AM–GM the $n-6$ factors $3,\dots,n-4$ (average $\frac{n-1}2$) give at most $\left(\frac{n-1}2\right)^{n-6}$. Hence
$$n!\le2(n-1)^4\left(\frac{n-1}2\right)^{n-6}=\frac{64}{n-1}\left(\frac{n-1}2\right)^{n-1}<\left(\frac{n-1}2\right)^{n-1}.$$
So $a^{n-1}<n!$ forces $a<\frac{n-1}2$, and likewise $b,c<\frac{n-1}2$.

**$n$ odd.** Then $a^{n-1},b^{n-1},c^{n-1}$ are squares, each $\equiv0$ or $1\pmod4$, and their sum $n!\equiv0\pmod4$; so all three are $\equiv0\pmod 4$, i.e. $a,b,c$ are even. Then $2^{n-1}\mid n!$. But $v_2(n!)=v_2((n-1)!)<n-1$ by ($\heartsuit$). Contradiction.

**$n$ even, all of $a+b,\,b+c,\,c+a$ powers of $2$.** Then $a,b,c$ have the same parity. If all are odd, the right side is odd while $n!$ is even. If all are divisible by $4$, then $4^{n-1}\mid n!$, contradicting $v_2(n!)<n$. So one of them, say $a$, is $\equiv2\pmod4$ (all are even). Then $2a=(a+b)+(a+c)-(b+c)$ is not divisible by $8$; as these three sums are powers of $2$ and at least $4$, one of them equals $4$, so two of the numbers equal $2$. By symmetry of the equation let these be two numbers equal to $2$ and the third $c'$ with $c'+2=2^s$. As $c'<n$, $c'\mid n!$ and $c'\mid c'^{n-1}$, hence $c'\mid2^{n-1}+2^{n-1}=2^n$. Then $\frac{c'}2=2^{s-1}-1$ (with $s\ge2$) is an odd divisor of $2^{n-1}$, so it equals $1$ and $c'=2$. Then $n!=3\cdot2^{n-1}$, impossible modulo $5$.

**$n$ even, some sum not a power of $2$.** Say $a+b$ has an odd prime factor $p$. Then $p\le a+b<n-1$. Since $n-1$ is odd, $a+b\mid a^{n-1}+b^{n-1}$, so $p\mid a^{n-1}+b^{n-1}$; also $p\mid n!$; hence $p\mid c^{n-1}$ and $p\mid c$. If $p\mid a$, then $p\mid b$ too and $p^{n-1}\mid n!$, contradicting $v_p(n!)<\frac n{p-1}\le\frac n2$. So $p\nmid ab$, and the lifting-the-exponent lemma (odd $p$, $p\mid a+b$, $p\nmid ab$, odd exponent) gives
$$v_p\big(a^{n-1}+b^{n-1}\big)=v_p(a+b)+v_p(n-1).$$
Moreover $v_p(c^{n-1})\ge n-1>\frac n2>v_p(n!)$, so $v_p\big(n!-c^{n-1}\big)=v_p(n!)$. Therefore
$$v_p(1)+v_p(2)+\dots+v_p(n)=v_p(n!)=v_p(a+b)+v_p(n-1).$$
Since $a+b$ and $n-1$ are two different numbers in $\{1,\dots,n\}$, no other number in $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is divisible by $p$. But $p\le c<\frac n2$, so $p$ and $2p$ are both multiples of $p$ in $\{1,\dots,n\}$; hence $\{p,2p\}=\{a+b,n-1\}$, and as $a+b<n-1$, $n-1=2p$ is even — contradicting that $n$ is even.

So no solution has $n>100$, and there are only finitely many quadruples. ∎

imo-isl-2021-n6.title: A counterexample, a shifting lemma, and induction via a partition lemma
imo-isl-2021-n6.body:
For a set $S$ of $n$ distinct integers let $s$ be its sum, and for an arrangement $(a_i)$ write $\Phi=\sum_{i=1}^n ia_i$.

**$n=2^ka$ with $a\ge3$ odd, $k\ge1$, fails.** Take the $n$ distinct numbers $1,1+n,1+2n,\dots,1+(n-2)n$ and $2^k+1$. Their sum is $\equiv(n-1)+2^k+1\equiv2^k\not\equiv0\pmod n$. All of them are $\equiv1\pmod{2^k}$, so for every arrangement
$$\Phi\equiv1+2+\dots+n=2^{k-1}a(2^ka+1)\pmod{2^k},$$
and $a(2^ka+1)$ is odd, so $2^k\nmid\Phi$ and $n\nmid\Phi$.

From now on $n$ is odd or a power of $2$.

**Lemma 1 (shifting).** If some arrangement has $\gcd(n,s)\mid\Phi$, then some arrangement has $n\mid\Phi$.
*Proof.* Let $\Phi_0=\sum ia_i$ and consider the cyclic shift $b_i=a_{i+x}$ (indices mod $n$). Then $\sum ib_i\equiv\sum_j(j-x)a_j=\Phi_0-xs\pmod n$, and $xs\equiv\Phi_0\pmod n$ is solvable in $x$ because $\gcd(n,s)\mid\Phi_0$. $\square$

**Lemma 2 (partition).** Let $m\ge2$, $k\ge1$. Every set $T$ of $km$ integers can be partitioned into $m$ sets of $k$ elements each, such that every part either has sum not divisible by $k$ or consists of numbers all congruent modulo $k$.
*Proof.* Induction on $m$. For $k=1$ everything is congruent mod $1$; let $k\ge2$.

*$m=2$.* If $k$ elements of $T$ are congruent mod $k$, let $A$ be such $k$ elements and $B=T\setminus A$. If $k\nmid\sum B$ we are done. Otherwise, if some $\beta\in B$ is not congruent to the elements of $A$, swap it with any $\alpha\in A$: the new sums are $\sum A+\beta-\alpha\equiv\beta-\alpha$ (as $\sum A\equiv k\alpha\equiv0$) and $\sum B-\beta+\alpha\equiv\alpha-\beta$, both non-zero mod $k$. If no such $\beta$ exists, all of $T$ is congruent mod $k$ and any partition works. If no $k$ elements are congruent mod $k$, then $T$ (with $2k$ elements) has three elements $a,b,c$ with distinct residues. Let $t=\sum T$ and take any $U\subseteq T\setminus\{a,b,c\}$ with $|U|=k-1$. The sums of $U\cup\{a\}$, $U\cup\{b\}$, $U\cup\{c\}$ have three distinct residues, so one of them, $A$, has $\sum A\not\equiv0,t$; then $A$ and $T\setminus A$ both have sums not divisible by $k$.

*$m>2$.* If $k$ elements are congruent mod $k$, take them as one part and apply induction to the rest. Otherwise pick any $U\subseteq T$ with $|U|=k-1$; not all of the $km-k+1\ge k$ remaining elements are $\equiv-\sum U\pmod k$, so some $a$ makes $\sum(U\cup\{a\})\not\equiv0$; take $U\cup\{a\}$ as a part and apply induction to the rest. $\square$

**Main proof (strong induction on $n$).** Let $S$ have $n\nmid s$.

*$n$ prime.* $\gcd(n,s)=1$ divides every $\Phi$; apply Lemma 1.

*$n$ composite.* Choose a prime $p$ with $v_p(s)<v_p(n)$ and put $k=n/p\ge2$; $k$ is odd if $n$ is odd and a power of $2$ if $n$ is. Then $\gcd(n,s)\mid k$ (the $p$-part of $\gcd(n,s)$ is at most $p^{v_p(n)-1}$). By Lemma 1 it suffices to find an arrangement with $k\mid\Phi$. By Lemma 2 split $S$ into $p$ parts of size $k$; call a part of the first kind if its sum is not divisible by $k$ (then by the induction hypothesis it has an arrangement $(c_1,\dots,c_k)$ with $k\mid\sum ic_i$), and of the second kind if all its elements are congruent mod $k$, say to $\rho$ (then its sum is $\equiv k\rho\equiv0\pmod k$, and any arrangement has $\sum_{i=1}^k ic_i\equiv\rho\frac{k(k+1)}2\pmod k$).

- *$n$ odd.* Then $k$ is odd, $\frac{k(k+1)}2\equiv0\pmod k$, so every part has an arrangement with $k\mid\sum ic_i$. Put the parts one after another in blocks of positions $jk+1,\dots,jk+k$; since $\sum_i(jk+i)c_i\equiv\sum_i ic_i\pmod k$, we get $k\mid\Phi$.
- *$n=2^e$, $e\ge2$.* Here $p=2$, $k=2^{e-1}$, two parts $U,V$. If both are of the first kind, concatenate them as above to get $k\mid\Phi$. Otherwise let $U$ be of the second kind; for it $\sum ic_i\equiv\rho\frac k2(k+1)\equiv0\pmod{k/2}$ and $\sum U\equiv0\pmod k$. Arrange $V$ as $(e_1,\dots,e_k)$ with $\frac k2\mid\sum ie_i$ (possible in either kind). Place $U$ at the odd positions $1,3,\dots,2k-1$ and $V$ at the even positions $2,4,\dots,2k$:
$$\Phi=\sum_{i=1}^k(2i-1)c_i+\sum_{i=1}^k2ie_i=2\sum ic_i-\sum U+2\sum ie_i\equiv0\pmod k.$$

In all cases $k\mid\Phi$ for some arrangement, and Lemma 1 finishes the induction.

**Answer: all odd $n$ and all powers of $2$.** ∎

*Remark.* The condition $n\nmid s$ cannot be dropped: the set $\{1,-1\}$ together with $n-2$ distinct multiples of $n$ admits no good arrangement.

imo-isl-2021-n7.title: Boundedness and arithmetic progressions of divisibility
imo-isl-2021-n7.body:
**Lemma 1.** Let $n>2m$. If $d\mid a_n$ and $d\mid a_{n-m}$, then $d\mid a_{n-2m}$; if $d\mid a_n$ and $d\mid a_{n-2m}$, then $d\mid a_{n-m}$.
*Proof.* $a_n\mid a_{n-2m}+a_{n-m}$ (the condition with index $n-2m$ and step $m$), so $d$ divides $a_{n-2m}+a_{n-m}$. $\square$

**Claim: $(a_n)$ is bounded.** Otherwise there are infinitely many records $a_n=k>a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$; take one with $n>10$. For $1\le s<\frac n2$, $k\mid a_{n-2s}+a_{n-s}$ and $0<a_{n-2s}+a_{n-s}<2k$, so $a_{n-s}+a_{n-2s}=k$. Using $s=1,2,4$: $a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}=a_{n-2}+a_{n-4}=a_{n-4}+a_{n-8}=k$, so $a_{n-1}=a_{n-4}$ and $a_{n-2}=a_{n-8}$. By Lemma 1 (first part, repeatedly, with $m=3$), $a_{n-1}$ divides $a_{n-1-3j}$ for all $j$ with $n-1-3j\ge1$; in particular $a_{n-1}\le\max(a_1,a_2,a_3)$. Similarly (with $m=6$) $a_{n-2}\le\max(a_1,\dots,a_6)$. Hence $k=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}\le2\max(a_1,\dots,a_6)$, which fails for large records. $\square$

**Truncation.** The sequence takes finitely many values; those occurring only finitely often all occur before some index $N$. The sequence $(a_{N+j})_{j\ge1}$ satisfies the same condition, and it suffices to show it is eventually periodic. So assume every value occurs infinitely often. Let $K$ be the largest value.

**Lemma 2.** If $d$ divides some term, then $I_d=\{i:d\mid a_i\}$ is an infinite arithmetic progression with odd difference.
*Proof.* $I_d$ is infinite since the divisible term recurs. Let $i_1<i_2<\dots$ be its elements. If $i_s+i_{s+1}$ were even, Lemma 1 (second part, with $m=\frac{i_{s+1}-i_s}2$) would give $d\mid a_{(i_s+i_{s+1})/2}$, an index strictly between two consecutive elements — impossible. So consecutive elements have different parities, and $i_s+i_{s+2}$ is even; Lemma 1 then gives $d\mid a_{(i_s+i_{s+2})/2}$, and the only element of $I_d$ strictly between $i_s$ and $i_{s+2}$ is $i_{s+1}$. Hence $i_{s+1}=\frac{i_s+i_{s+2}}2$: $I_d$ is an arithmetic progression, with odd difference. $\square$

**Conclusion.** Let $\mathcal D$ be the finite set of positive integers dividing at least one term (all are $\le K$). For $d\in\mathcal D$ let $I_d$ have first element $f_d$ and difference $\delta_d$, and put $D=\prod_{d\in\mathcal D}\delta_d$ and $N_0=\max f_d$. For $n\ge N_0$ and $d\in\mathcal D$: $n\in I_d\iff n+D\in I_d$. So for $n\ge N_0$ the terms $a_n$ and $a_{n+D}$ have the same divisors (every divisor of either lies in $\mathcal D$), hence $a_n=a_{n+D}$ (each is its own largest divisor). So the sequence is eventually periodic with period $D$. ∎

imo-isl-2021-n8.title: Constructions; CRT for two coprime factors; Hensel-type analysis for odd prime powers
imo-isl-2021-n8.body:
Regard $P$ as a map $\mathbb Z_\ell\to\mathbb Z_\ell$ (residues mod $\ell$) and let $f_{m,\ell}=|P^m(\mathbb Z_\ell)|$, $f_{0,\ell}=\ell$. As $1,\dots,n$ is a complete residue system, the condition says $f_{m,n}=\lceil n/2^m\rceil$ for $m\ge1$, equivalently $f_{m+1,n}=\lceil f_{m,n}/2\rceil$ for all $m\ge0$. Two general facts:
- $P^{m+1}(\mathbb Z_\ell)\subseteq P^m(\mathbb Z_\ell)$, and if $f_{m+1,\ell}=f_{m,\ell}$ then $P$ permutes $P^m(\mathbb Z_\ell)$ and $f_{j,\ell}=f_{m,\ell}$ for all $j\ge m$. *(Stabilisation.)*
- Under the condition, $f_{m,n}=1$ for large $m$, hence also $f_{m,d}=1$ for every $d\mid n$ (reduction mod $d$ maps $P^m(\mathbb Z_n)$ onto $P^m(\mathbb Z_d)$).

**Part 1: powers of $2$ and primes work.** For $n=2^k$ take $P(x)=2x$: $P^m(\mathbb Z_{2^k})=2^m\mathbb Z_{2^k}$ has $\lceil2^k/2^m\rceil$ elements. For an odd prime $p$, every function $\mathbb Z_p\to\mathbb Z_p$ is given by an integer polynomial (Lagrange interpolation over $\mathbb F_p$); take the one sending $x\in\{0,\dots,p-1\}$ to $\lfloor x/2\rfloor$. It maps $\{0,\dots,N-1\}$ onto $\{0,\dots,\lceil N/2\rceil-1\}$, so $f_{m,p}=\lceil p/2^m\rceil$. ($n=1$ is trivial.)

**Part 2: $n=ab$ with coprime $a,b>1$ fails.** By the Chinese remainder theorem $f_{m,ab}=f_{m,a}f_{m,b}$. By stabilisation and $f_{m,a}\to1$: for every $m$, $f_{m+1,a}<f_{m,a}$ unless $f_{m,a}=1$; same for $b$. Let $m$ be minimal with $f_{m+1,a}=1$ or $f_{m+1,b}=1$, say $f_{m+1,a}=1$. Then $f_{m,a}\ge2$ and $f_{m,b}\ge2$ (also for $m=0$), so $f_{m+1,b}<f_{m,b}$ and
$$f_{m+1,ab}=f_{m+1,b}<f_{m,b}\le\frac{f_{m,a}f_{m,b}}2=\frac{f_{m,ab}}2\le\left\lceil\frac{f_{m,ab}}2\right\rceil=f_{m+1,ab},$$
a contradiction.

**Part 3: $n=p^k$, $p$ odd prime, $k\ge2$, fails.** For $r\in\mathbb Z_p$ let $S_r\subseteq\mathbb Z_{p^k}$ be the residues $\equiv r\pmod p$; $|S_r|=p^{k-1}$ and $P(S_r)\subseteq S_{P(r)}$. Recall $P(x+h)=P(x)+hP'(x)+h^2Q(x,h)$ with $Q$ an integer polynomial.

*Claim.* $|P(S_r)|=p^{k-1}$ (then $P(S_r)=S_{P(r)}$) or $|P(S_r)|\le p^{k-2}$.
If $p\mid P'(r)$, then $P(r+ps)\equiv P(r)\pmod{p^2}$, so $P(S_r)$ lies in one class mod $p^2$, of size $p^{k-2}$. If $p\nmid P'(r)$, $P$ is injective on $S_r$: for $x\ne y$ in $S_r$ with $h=y-x$, $1\le v_p(h)<k$, we get $v_p(hP'(x))=v_p(h)<v_p(h^2Q)$, so $v_p(P(y)-P(x))=v_p(h)<k$. $\square$

Iterating, each $|P^j(S_r)|$ is either $p^{k-1}$ (a full class) or $\le p^{k-2}$, and once small it stays small. Since $f_{j,p^k}\to1$, let $m\ge1$ be minimal with $|P^m(S_q)|\le p^{k-2}$ for all $q$; then some $r$ has $P^{m-1}(S_r)$ a full class. Let
$$\alpha=\big|P^m(\mathbb Z_{p^k})\setminus P^m(S_r)\big|.$$
Every element of this set is $P$ of an element of $P^{m-1}(\mathbb Z_{p^k})\setminus P^{m-1}(S_r)$, so $\alpha\le f_{m-1}-p^{k-1}$ (writing $f_j=f_{j,p^k}$). With $f_{m-1}\le2f_m$ and $f_m\le p^{k-2}+\alpha$:
$$\alpha+p^{k-1}\le2p^{k-2}+2\alpha,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\alpha\ge(p-2)p^{k-2}>0.\tag{1}$$

*Dynamics mod $p$.* As $f_{j,p}\to1$, $P$ has exactly one fixed point $t$ mod $p$, and the sets $A_j=\{s\in\mathbb Z_p:P^j(s)\equiv t\}$ increase strictly until they equal $\mathbb Z_p$ (if $A_j=A_{j+1}$ then $A_{j+1}=A_{j+2}$). As $|A_0|=1$, either $A_{m-1}=\mathbb Z_p$ or $|A_{m-1}|\ge m$.
- If $A_{m-1}=\mathbb Z_p$, then $P^{m-1}(\mathbb Z_{p^k})\subseteq S_t$ has at most $p^{k-1}=|P^{m-1}(S_r)|$ elements, so it equals $P^{m-1}(S_r)$ and $\alpha=0$, contradicting (1).
- Otherwise let $X=A_{m-1}$ ($|X|\ge m$), $Y=\bigcup_{q\in X}S_q$, $Z=\bigcup_{q\notin X}S_q$. Note $P(S_t)\subseteq S_t$ and $P(S_t)\ne S_t$ (else $|P^m(S_t)|=p^{k-1}$), so $|P(S_t)|\le p^{k-2}$ by the Claim. Since $P^{m-1}(Y)\subseteq S_t$, $|P^m(Y)|\le p^{k-2}$, and $|P^m(Z)|\le(p-m)p^{k-2}$. Thus
$$(p-2)p^{k-2}\le\alpha<f_m\le(p-m+1)p^{k-2},$$
so $m\le2$. Then $|P^2(S_q)|\le p^{k-2}$ for all $q$, whence $\frac{p^k}4\le f_2\le p^{k-1}$ and $p\le4$, i.e. $p=3$.

*The case $p=3$.* Let $t$ be the fixed point mod $3$. As shown, $P(S_t)\ne S_t$, so by the Claim's proof $3\mid P'(t)$. Then by induction on $i$ all elements of $P^i(S_t)$ are congruent mod $3^{i+1}$: if $y=x+h$ with $3^{i+1}\mid h$ and $x\in S_t$, then $3\mid P'(x)$ and $P(y)\equiv P(x)\pmod{3^{i+2}}$. Hence $|P^{k-1}(S_t)|=1$. Also $f_{1,3}\le2$ (otherwise $P$ permutes $\mathbb Z_3$ forever) and then $f_{2,3}\le1$ by stabilisation, so $P^2(\mathbb Z_{3^k})\subseteq S_t$ and $f_{k+1,3^k}\le|P^{k-1}(S_t)|=1$. But the condition requires $f_{k+1,3^k}=\lceil3^k/2^{k+1}\rceil\ge2$, since $3^k>2^{k+1}$ for $k\ge2$. Contradiction.

**Conclusion.** By Parts 2 and 3, $n$ must be a power of $2$ or a prime, and Part 1 shows these work.

**Answer: all powers of $2$ (including $1$) and all primes.** ∎
